newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn debt level precarious due to unification - Buba.
newsitem.headline: Bonn debt level precarious due to unification - Buba.

text.p: Germany's public debt has more than doubled to 2.135 trillion marks between 1989 and the end of 1996, but more than half the increase results from the cost of unification in 1990, the Bundesbank said on Tuesday.

Warning that Germany's public finances were in a "precarious" state and not sustainable, the central bank said the government must adhere strictly to its course of fiscal consolidation to avoid falling into a "debt trap" and to qualify for Europe's planned monetary union.

The bank said in its March monthly report that Germany's public debt as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP) had risen to 60.3 percent at the end of 1996, slightly above the 60 percent ceiling set by the Maastricht Treaty for countries seeking to join monetary union.
In 1989, one year before unification, the debt-to-GDP ratio had been 41.8 percent with a debt level of 929 billion marks.

Of the 1.2 trillion-mark rise in Germany's public debt since 1989, more than half resulted from taking over the liabilities of the former communist east German state and from funding the modernisation of its economy, the report said.
"The conclusion is that the only way out of the current precarious debt situation lies in a convincing consolidation strategy," the Bundesbank said.
It added that Germany could only afford for a limited period to fund unification through increased debt.
"Otherwise it risks falling into a debt trap in which the state deficit and state debt will feed each other through rapidly rising interest burdens."
It was a "warning sign" that that the rise in the debt-to-GDP ratio in recent years had resulted largely from the high interest rate burden, the Bundesbank said.
The bank also criticised the government for underestimating the fiscal burden of unification and failing initially to adapt properly to the new situation in its tax and spending policies.

But it noted that despite having to shoulder the cost of unification, Germany's debt ratio rose at a slower pace than the average of all European Union countries over the period and lagged well behind the debt increases on France and Italy.

A convincing consolidation strategy would not only directly slow down the rise in public debt but would also contribute to keeping interest rates low and thereby boost economic growth, the Bundesbank said.
